description: Published, source-backed trivia. Selection is local; this is not live AI generation.

facts.title: A year before a full turn.
facts.text: One Venus rotation takes 243 Earth days, while its orbit around the Sun completes in 225 Earth days. A full rotation takes longer than its year.
facts.evidence: One Venus rotation takes 243 Earth days; one orbit takes 225 Earth days.
facts.authorship: Ollama llama3.2:latest draft, edited and checked against NASA before publication

facts.title: Sunrise goes the other way.
facts.text: On Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east. The planet rotates in the opposite direction to Earth.
facts.evidence: Venus rotates backward relative to Earth, so the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: The hottest planet isn’t the closest.
facts.text: Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun. Its thick atmosphere traps heat through a runaway greenhouse effect.
facts.evidence: Venus is the hottest planet; its thick atmosphere traps heat through a runaway greenhouse effect.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A planet that rolls on its side.
facts.text: Uranus has an axial tilt of about 98 degrees. Its unusual orientation means one pole can spend roughly 21 Earth years in a dark winter.
facts.evidence: Uranus has a 97.77-degree tilt; one half experiences a 21-year-long dark winter.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A little methane, a lot of color.
facts.text: Methane in Uranus’s atmosphere absorbs red light. That helps give the planet its blue-green appearance.
facts.evidence: Methane absorbs the red portion of sunlight, producing Uranus’s blue-green color.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Mars is wearing rust.
facts.text: Mars looks red because iron minerals in its rocks and dust oxidize. The familiar color of the Red Planet comes from rust.
facts.evidence: Oxidized iron in Martian rocks, soil, and dust makes Mars appear red.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: The solar system’s biggest volcano.
facts.text: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in our solar system. Its enormous base covers an area comparable to the US state of Arizona.
facts.evidence: Olympus Mons is the largest solar-system volcano, with a base roughly the area of Arizona.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Potato-shaped moons.
facts.text: Mars’s two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, are irregular rather than round. They have too little mass for gravity to pull them into spheres.
facts.evidence: Phobos and Deimos have too little mass for gravity to make them spherical.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A Martian day has its own name.
facts.text: A day on Mars is called a sol and lasts about 24.6 hours. Its day is close to ours, but a Martian year lasts about 687 Earth days.
facts.evidence: Mars rotates every 24.6 hours; its year equals 687 Earth days, and its days are called sols.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A giant with surprisingly low density.
facts.text: Saturn is the only planet in our solar system whose average density is lower than water’s. The familiar “floating planet” idea is a comparison of densities, not a real experiment.
facts.evidence: Saturn alone among solar-system planets has an average density below water.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Those rings aren’t solid hoops.
facts.text: Saturn’s rings consist of billions of pieces of ice and rock. Many are tiny grains, while some particles are as large as mountains.
facts.evidence: Saturn’s rings contain billions of ice and rock pieces, from grains to mountain-sized particles.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A scorching day, a freezing night.
facts.text: Mercury’s surface can reach about 430°C by day and fall to around −180°C at night. It has no substantial atmosphere to hold onto the daytime heat.
facts.evidence: Mercury reaches about 430°C by day and −180°C at night, lacking an atmosphere that retains heat.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Wind faster than a jetliner.
facts.text: Neptune’s winds can exceed 2,000 kilometers per hour. Even far from the Sun, this planet has the fastest winds in our solar system.
facts.evidence: Neptune is the windiest solar-system planet, with winds exceeding 2,000 km/h.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: One orbit takes generations.
facts.text: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun. In 2011 it completed its first orbit since its discovery in 1846.
facts.evidence: Neptune completed its first 165-year orbit since its 1846 discovery in 2011.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Three hearts, one octopus.
facts.text: An octopus has three hearts. Two move blood through the gills, while the third pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of its body.

source.title: Cephalopods: Octopus, Squid, Cuttlefish, and Nautilus

facts.evidence: Two branchial hearts move blood through the gills; a systemic heart circulates oxygenated blood through the body.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Blue blood without the royalty.
facts.text: Octopuses use a copper-based molecule called hemocyanin to transport oxygen. Their blood is blue, unlike our iron-based red blood.

source.title: Cephalopods: Octopus, Squid, Cuttlefish, and Nautilus

facts.evidence: Cephalopod blood is blue and transports oxygen using copper-based hemocyanin.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: An underwater impersonator.
facts.text: The mimic octopus can change both its appearance and its movements to resemble other sea creatures, including flounders, lionfish, and sea snakes.

source.title: How Octopuses and Squids Change Color

facts.evidence: The mimic octopus changes skin color and movement to imitate species including flounders, lionfish, and sea snakes.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Tiny ocean life, enormous oxygen production.
facts.text: Scientists estimate that ocean organisms produce roughly half of Earth’s oxygen. Much of that production comes from plankton; marine life also consumes roughly as much oxygen as the ocean produces.

source.title: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?

facts.evidence: Roughly half of oxygen production occurs in the ocean, largely from plankton; marine life consumes about as much.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: The ocean has a twilight zone.
facts.text: The layer about 200 to 1,000 meters below the ocean’s surface is called the twilight zone. There is some light, but too little for photosynthesis.

source.title: How far does light travel in the ocean?

facts.evidence: The dysphotic or twilight zone extends from 200 to 1,000 meters; its light is insufficient for photosynthesis.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Sunlight has a depth limit.
facts.text: Below about 1,000 meters, sunlight does not penetrate the ocean. This sunless region is called the aphotic zone.

source.title: How far does light travel in the ocean?

facts.evidence: The aphotic zone below 1,000 meters receives no penetrating sunlight.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: The sea gets salt from land.
facts.text: Rainwater slowly erodes rocks, releasing dissolved ions that rivers carry into the ocean. Seafloor openings and volcanic activity also add salts.
facts.evidence: Ocean salts come from weathered land rocks and seafloor sources, including hydrothermal and volcanic activity.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Seawater has a measurable recipe.
facts.text: On average, dissolved salts make up about 3.5% of seawater’s weight. That amount varies with processes such as evaporation and rainfall.
facts.evidence: Average seawater salinity is about 35 parts per thousand by weight, varying with evaporation and precipitation.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Water filters the light.
facts.text: Ocean water absorbs light from the red part of the spectrum, leaving more blue light visible. Floating particles can also give the water green, red, or other hues.
facts.evidence: Water absorbs red wavelengths; sediments and particles can modify the ocean’s visible color.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A living tower, more than 100 meters tall.
facts.text: Coast redwoods can grow more than 350 feet tall. They are the world’s tallest tree species.
facts.evidence: Coast redwoods exceed 350 feet in height and are the tallest trees.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Some redwoods were seedlings two millennia ago.
facts.text: Coast redwoods can live for around 2,000 years. Their extraordinary lifespan accompanies their extraordinary height.
facts.evidence: Some of the oldest living coast redwoods were seedlings 2,000 years ago.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: An enormous tree, measured by volume.
facts.text: The General Sherman Tree is the world?s largest tree by volume. This giant sequoia contains roughly 1,487 cubic meters of wood in its trunk.

source.title: The Largest Trees in the World

facts.evidence: The General Sherman Tree is the largest tree by volume, measured at 1,487 cubic meters.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: A banana is a berry in botany.
facts.text: Botanical categories do not always match kitchen labels. A banana fruit is classified as a berry.
facts.evidence: Kew describes banana fruit as a berry in botanical terminology.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Vanilla comes from an orchid.
facts.text: Vanilla planifolia is an orchid and a source of natural vanilla. The vanilla orchid at Kew is hand-pollinated to produce pods.
facts.evidence: Vanilla planifolia supplies vanilla; Kew hand-pollinates its vanilla orchid to produce pods.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: An atom can keep the beat.
facts.text: Atomic clocks keep time using frequencies associated with atoms. The first atomic clock was built in 1949 at the institution now known as NIST.
facts.evidence: The first atomic clock was invented in 1949 by National Bureau of Standards scientists.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: Your navigation depends on timekeeping in space.
facts.text: Every GPS satellite carries multiple atomic clocks. Their precise timing data is part of what makes satellite navigation possible.
facts.evidence: Each GPS satellite has multiple atomic clocks supplying precise time data to GPS signals.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: One computer bug really was a bug.
facts.text: In 1947, engineers working on Harvard’s Mark II computer found a moth inside a component. They taped the insect into their logbook, which is now in the Smithsonian’s collection.

source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
source.title: Log Book With Computer Bug

facts.evidence: Mark II engineers found a moth in a component in 1947 and taped it into their logbook.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication

facts.title: One decree, three scripts.
facts.text: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek writing. These parallel inscriptions helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
facts.evidence: The decree appears in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek scripts; the parallel text aided decipherment.
facts.authorship: AI-assisted editorial draft; source checked before publication
